stages.name: QE and asset bubbles
stages.title: QE and asset bubbles
stages.sub: Why pumping money into the economy through QE can end up widening inequality rather than closing it.

steps.q: A central bank creates new money and uses it to buy up large quantities of government bonds and other financial assets. What happens to the amount of money in the economy?
steps.hint: The bank is creating new money to spend on assets, not swapping existing money around.
steps.pre: So new money enters the economy through

steps.q: The central bank is now a huge buyer of bonds and shares, competing with everyone else who wants them. What tends to happen to the price of those assets?
steps.hint: If demand for something jumps while the amount available barely changes, what happens to its price?

steps.q: Shares, bonds and property that just became more valuable are mostly held by wealthier households, not by people with little savings. Who benefits most as these prices climb?
steps.wrong: Those with little or no savings
steps.hint: You can only gain from a price rise in something you actually hold.

steps.q: Wealthier asset-owning households get richer while low-income households, who own few assets, see little benefit. What does this do to the gap between rich and poor?
steps.hint: Think about who gained from rising asset prices and who was left out.
